Mason's nerine is a diminutive, critically endangered Eastern Cape species with narrow, thread-like evergreen foliage that forms dense clumps of wiry stems topped with small umbels of up to a dozen wavy-edged, pale-to-deep pink flowers, opening in late summer ahead of most other nerines. It is among the hardiest and most drought-tolerant nerines once established, tolerating colder and drier conditions than the showier hybrid guernsey lilies, and suits a rock garden, trough, or raised bed where its small scale can be appreciated up close. Leave clumps undisturbed for years, since flowering improves as the bulbs become congested.

planting.note: Plant bulbs with the neck at soil level in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing clumps to allow for its spreading, grassy habit.

directions: Plant bulbs with the neck at soil level in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun. Thread-leaf nerine forms low, evergreen tufts of very narrow, thread-like leaves and sends up wiry scapes carrying loose umbels of small, funnel-shaped, wavy-petaled pink to rosy-red flowers in late summer and early fall. Considered one of the hardiest and most reliably floriferous of the dwarf nerine species, it spreads gradually by offsets into a dense, groundcover-like patch and tolerates drought once established. In colder parts of its range mulch heavily over winter or grow in a trough or pot that can be sheltered.

planting.note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in fall in well-drained, average to sandy soil in full sun.

directions: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in fall in well-drained, average to sandy soil in full sun. Arderne's White is a long-cultivated white-flowered selection of the pink Cape watsonia, carrying the same tall, gladiolus-like spikes of large, funnel-shaped flowers but in clean white with only a faint blush, above broad, glossy, sword-shaped fans of foliage. It has been grown in mild-winter gardens for generations as a striking contrast to the species' more common pink and lavender-pink forms, and it shares the same wet-winter, dry-summer growth cycle, resting dormant through the hottest months. Established clumps multiply readily by cormlets and are best left undisturbed for several years to build up flowering size.

planting.note: Plant corms 4-5 inches deep in fall in stony or clay-loam, well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: Plant corms 4-5 inches deep in fall in stony or clay-loam, well-drained soil in full sun. Fragrant bugle lily produces broad, blue-green, yellow-margined sword-shaped leaves and, in spring, tall branching spikes bearing dense ranks of thirty or more cup-shaped, sweetly fragrant flowers in shades of pink to dark red or occasionally white. It is one of the larger and showier watsonia species, reaching well over four feet in bloom, and like other winter-rainfall Cape watsonias it requires a completely dry rest through summer. Give it a sunny, open position with excellent drainage and withhold water entirely once the foliage begins to yellow after flowering.

planting.note: Plant corms 2-3 inches deep in fall in well-drained, clay-loam to sandy soil in full sun in mild-winter zones.

directions: Plant corms 2-3 inches deep in fall in well-drained, clay-loam to sandy soil in full sun in mild-winter zones. Pale harlequin flower is a Cape winter-rainfall species distinguished from the common Sparaxis tricolor by its salmon-pink to white flowers, each marked at the throat with a bold ring of yellow and black and set off by unusual purple, S-shaped anthers curled tightly around the style. It grows and flowers through the cool season on a compact fan of lance-shaped leaves before going dormant for a dry summer rest, and naturalizes well in Mediterranean-climate gardens where the soil dries out after bloom. Plant in generous drifts for the best display, and lift and store corms where summers are wet or winters harsher than zone 8.

planting.note: Plant bulbs after last frost in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade.

directions: Plant bulbs after last frost in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade, ideal for a raised bed, rock garden, or container where its unusual scale can be appreciated. Dwarf wide-leaf pineapple lily is a high-elevation Drakensberg species with the widest leaves of any eucomis relative to its size — broad, wavy-edged, purple-spotted foliage only a few inches tall — topped in midsummer by a short, purple-flecked flower spike of greenish-white, purple-tinted flowers crowned with the characteristic leafy pineapple-top bracts. Despite its montane origin it is remarkably drought-tolerant in cultivation and, being smaller in every dimension than the common garden pineapple lilies, suits a prominent spot at the front of a border. Reduce watering once the foliage yellows in fall to let the bulb enter winter dormancy, and mulch in colder parts of its range.

planting.note: Plant corms 2-3 inches deep in fall in well-drained, sandy soil in full sun to bright, open shade.

directions: Plant corms 2-3 inches deep in fall in well-drained, sandy soil in full sun to bright, open shade. Cream freesia bears the same wiry, arching stems and narrow, sword-shaped leaves as garden freesia hybrids but with strongly sweet-scented, cream to pale yellow flowers marked deep yellow-orange in the throat, blooming in spring on a Mediterranean growth cycle of fall planting and summer dormancy. It is one of the principal wild parents behind many modern yellow-flowered freesia hybrids, valued in its own right for its fragrance and drought tolerance once established. In frost-free gardens leave corms in the ground to naturalize; elsewhere lift after the foliage dies back, dry, and store cool until fall replanting.
